etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Tamil 𑀢𑀫𑀺𑀵𑁰 (tamiḻ).
According to Bhadriraju Krishnamurthi (2003), earlier recorded as Pali damiḷa. Further etymology unknown. Various hypotheses have been adduced. The main ones consider this word a compound of some sort:
* K. V. Zvelebil (1990) proposes that தமிழ் (tamiḻ) is derived from the verb தகு (taku, “to fit properly”) with the evolution tak- > tav- > tam-.
* Koskinen (1996) speculates a relationship with the name of the lotus flower தாமரை (tāmarai), attested also with the variant தம்மி (tammi), and having cognates in Malayalam താമര (tāmara), Kannada ತಾಮರೆ (tāmare), Tulu ತಾಮರೆ (tāmare) and Telugu తామర (tāmara).
* Southworth (1998) suggests a derivation like *tam-miẓ > tam-iḻ “one's own speech”, considering the final part as a reduced form of மொழி (moḻi, “word, speech”).
However, there are problems with each of these attempts. The sounds -k- and -v- are nowhere attested as variants; moreover, the underlying form of மொழி (moḻi) is Proto-Dravidian *moẓ-, not *miẓ-. The etymology of the word therefore remains unknown.

etymology_text:
Borrowed from English Madras, from Tamil மதராசப்பட்டினம் (matarācappaṭṭiṉam), attested in Vijayanagara-era inscriptions, equivalent to மதராசு (matarācu) + பட்டினம் (paṭṭiṉam). Some considered it to be a shortening of the phrase Portuguese Madre de Dios or Mãe de Deus, which translates to 'Mother of God,' referring to the St. Mary's Church due to Portuguese influence of the port city.
Alternative etymologies also include, Telugu ముఁదిరాజ్ (mun̆dirāj), from ముందిర్ (mundir) + రాజ్ (rāj). See Madras on Wikipedia for more.

glosses: Madras (former name of Chennai: the capital and largest city of Tamil Nadu, India)

etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Tamil 𑀇𑀮𑀓𑁆𑀓𑀡𑀫𑁆 (ilakkaṇam). From there, probably derived from a Prakrit, from Sanskrit लक्षण (lakṣaṇa); doublet of லக்ஷணம் (lakṣaṇam).
Another proposed etymology is from இலக்கு (ilakku, from இலங்கு (ilaṅku, “to be an example, standard”), distinct from the Sanskrit borrowing, compare துலங்கு (tulaṅku)) + அண் (aṇ, the proximal quality base, see அண்மை (aṇmai)) + அம் (am, “-ness”), which would translate to 'the standard (of language).' See இலக்கணம் - சொல்விளக்கம் on Tamil Wikipedia for more.

Cognate with Kannada ಅರಸ (arasa), ಅರಸು (arasu), Malayalam അരചൻ (aracaṉ), Telugu అరుసు (arusu), Tulu ಅರಸು (arasu).
Doublet of ராஜா (rājā), ராஜன் (rājaṉ), ராசன் (rācaṉ), and இராசன் (irācaṉ).

etymology_text:
Inherited from Proto-Dravidian *paẓam (“fruit”), from Proto-Dravidian *paẓV- (“to ripen, mature”). Equivalent to பழு (paḻu, “to ripen”) + -அம் (-am).
Cognates and doublets
Cognate with Irula பம்மு (pammu), Kannada ಹಣ್ಣು (haṇṇu), Kolami పండ్ (paṇḍ), Malayalam പഴം (paḻaṁ), Telugu పండు (paṇḍu). Doublet of பண்டம் (paṇṭam).
Compare Sanskrit फल (phala), borrowed from Dravidian, whence பலன் (palaṉ, “benefit”) and பலம் (palam). Compare also பயன் (payaṉ) and பயம் (payam).

etymology_text:
Uncertain. Possibly from Indo-Aryan. Compare Prakrit *𑀝𑀺𑀧𑁆𑀧𑀢𑀺 (*ṭippati, “notes”), *𑀝𑀺𑀧𑁆𑀧 (*ṭippa, “note”), Gujarati ટીપ (ṭīp), Marathi टीप (ṭīp, “note, list”), टापरणें (ṭāparṇẽ, “mallet”), टिपणें (ṭipṇẽ, “to jot; to hit”).
Cognate with Kannada ಟಪಾಲು (ṭapālu), ಟಪಾಲ (ṭapāla), Malayalam തപാൽ (tapāl), Telugu టపా (ṭapā), తపాలా (tapālā), టపాలు (ṭapālu). Later Indo-Aryan (re)borrowings are concentrated in the West and South (elsewhere dak is used): Deccani ٹَپّال (ṭappāl), ٹَپّا (ṭappā), Gujarati ટપાલ (ṭapāl), Konkani and Marathi टपाल (ṭapāl), Sindhi ٽَپالَ /टपाल (ṭapāla).
Alternatively, borrowed from Dutch de paal; compare Indonesian tapal.

etymology_text: Compound of தேவ (tēva, “godly, divine, sacred”, from Sanskrit देव (deva)) + அடியாள் (aṭiyāḷ, “(female) devotee, servant, follower”), translating to 'the divine servant' or 'devotee of the gods', referring to the women who underwent the Hindu religious practice of becoming a devadasi ("married" to a deity) in olden days. In addition to taking care of the temple, they were taught Bharatanatyam and other classical Indian arts, and enjoyed high social status. In latter days they were forced to get involved into sex work and be "pleasers" for the rich aristocrats and became synonymous with harlots and prostitutes. Cognate with Malayalam തേവടിയാൽ (tēvaṭiyāl).

etymology_text: From திருவெவ்வுளூர் (tiruvevvuḷūr), from திருஎவ்வுளூர் (tiru’evvuḷūr), compound of திரு (tiru) + எவ்வுள் (evvuḷ) + ஊர் (ūr). Attested in Middle Tamil works by Tirumalisai Alvar and Thirumangai Alvar as just எவ்வுள் (evvuḷ), considered to be a shortening of எவ் உள் உறங்கலாம்? (ev uḷ uṟaṅkalām?, “where do I sleep?”). See Tiruvallur in Wikipedia for more.

etymology_text:
Onomatopoeic. Compare Chinese 哎喲 /哎哟 (āiyō).
Cognates
Cognate with Kannada ಅಯ್ಯೋ (ayyō), Malayalam അയ്യോ (ayyō), Telugu అయ్యో (ayyō), Tulu ಅಯ್ಯೋ (ayyō).
Possibly related to ஐ (ai, “lord, master”), ஐயம் (aiyam), ஐயன் (aiyaṉ, “father, man of respect, etc”).

examples.text: தகப்பனை நோக்கி: ஏன் ஜநிப்பித்தாய் என்றும், தாயை நோக்கி: ஏன் பெற்றாய் என்றும் சொல்லுகிறவனுக்கு ஐயோ!
examples.ref: “ஏசாயா 45:10”, in TAOVBSI (Tamil Old Bible), Bible Society of India (BSI):
examples.english: Woe unto him that saith unto his father, What begettest thou? or to the woman, What hast thou brought forth?
examples.roman: takappaṉai nōkki: ēṉ janippittāy eṉṟum, tāyai nōkki: ēṉ peṟṟāy eṉṟum collukiṟavaṉukku aiyō!
examples.translation: Woe unto him that saith unto his father, What begettest thou? or to the woman, What hast thou brought forth?

glosses: an expression of pain, sorrow, regret, grief, concern, wonder, exasperation. (aiyo, woe, alas, ow, ouch, ew, bruh, sheesh)

etymology_text:
Cognate with Malayalam ചുക്ക് (cukkŭ, “dried ginger”).
Further information
Probably related to சுருங்கு (curuṅku, “to shrivel, contract”), சுருக்கு (curukku, “contraction; wrinkle”), Kannada ಸುಕ್ಕು (sukku, “to contract; to become dry; wrinkle”), Malayalam ചുക്കുക (cukkuka, “to grow dry, shrivel”), Telugu స్రుక్కు (srukku, “to shrink”).
Alternatively, borrowed from Prakrit 𑀲𑀼𑀓𑁆𑀔 (sukkha, “dry”). Compare Hindi सूखा (sūkhā, “dry”).

Further information

etymology_text: Borrowed from Hindi जलाई (jalāī). According to folk etymology, the term comes from a Tamil speaker, with little knowledge of Hindi, reading a sign near a toilet and assuming जलाई (jalāī) meant "to defecate". The sign is thought to have said "Inflammable objects not allowed - Jalaaishi padaarth mana hai". However, this is doubtful.

etymology_text: Uncertain; there are multiple theories, which includes உப்பு (uppu, “salt”) + தளம் (taḷam, “area, place”). When Sheikh Ibn Battuta landed in the Puttalam lagoon in 1344, he apparently mentioned a city called Pattala? in the area in his work, commonly known as al-Rihla. This town, as well as Puttalam district, was traditionally a Tamil area, which is why many of the place-names and rivers in the area have Tamil names.

examples.english: Is it my fate to wander around like this?

examples.text: 'அவரவர் தலையெழுத்துப்படி படிக்கட்டுமே' என்று அன்று இராசாசி கூறியதற்கு வெகுண்டெழுந்து, "தலையெழுத்தா ? எவனதை எழுதினான் கொண்டுவா; நான் அதை மாற்றி எழுதுகிறேன்" என்று ‘67 தேர்தலில் கூட்டந்தொறும் முழங்கி வந்தவர் […]
examples.ref: Perunchithiranar, வேண்டும் விடுதலை [(We) Need Freedom], published 2005:
examples.english: The one who had been thundering throughout the rallies for the 1967 election, furious at Rajaji's remark, 'let everyone study according to their fate [caste],' said, "Fate? Which guy wrote it? Bring it to me; I will rewrite it." […]
examples.roman: 'avaravar talaiyeḻuttuppaṭi paṭikkaṭṭumē' eṉṟu aṉṟu irācāci kūṟiyataṟku vekuṇṭeḻuntu, "talaiyeḻuttā ? evaṉatai eḻutiṉāṉ koṇṭuvā; nāṉ atai māṟṟi eḻutukiṟēṉ" eṉṟu ‘67 tērtalil kūṭṭantoṟum muḻaṅki vantavar […]

examples.text: அப்போது பேசிய அவர், 'எத்தனையோ பணிகள் இருந்தாலும் 2 பணிகள் தான் முக்கியமானதாக காலம் தொடர்ந்து பார்த்துக் கொள்கிறது. மருத்துவப்பணி பிணம் ஆகாமல் பார்த்துக் கொள்கிறது. ஆசிரியர் பணி நடைப்பிணம் ஆகாமல் பார்த்துக் கொள்கிறது.

examples.text: “தற்காலத்தில் சங்கி என்பது ஒரு குறிப்பிட்ட சித்தாந்தம் பேசக்கூடிய அரசியல் கட்சி சார்புள்ளவர்களைக் கூறுகிறார்கள். முன்பு, ஒரு சங்கத்தில், அமைப்பில் இருந்தவர்கள் தங்களை சங் உறுப்பினர் – சங்கி என அடையாளப்படுத்திக் கொண்டனர்,” என்றார்.
examples.ref: 2025 July 16, “தமிழ்நாட்டில் 'சங்கி' என்ற சொல் பரவலாகப் பயன்படுத்தப்படும் காரணமும் பின்னணியும் [tamiḻnāṭṭil 'caṅki' eṉṟa col paravalākap payaṉpaṭuttappaṭum kāraṇamum piṉṉaṇiyum, Reason and background of the widespread use of the term 'sanghi' in Tamil Nadu]”, in BBC Tamil, archived from the original on 31 Jan 2024:

etymology_text:
Cognate with Kannada ಪಿತ್ತಲಾಟ (pittalāṭa), Kota (India) [script needed] (pitlāṭm), Malayalam പിത്തലാട്ടം (pittalāṭṭaṁ), Telugu పితలాటకము (pitalāṭakamu).
The Tamil Lexicon dictionary proposes a Sanskritic origin from पित्तल (pittala, “brass”) + हाटक (hāṭaka, “gold”), as in "passing brass for gold"; compare பித்தலாடகம் (pittalāṭakam), பித்தளையாடகம் (pittaḷaiyāṭakam). Under this interpretation, the final element may have been reshaped under the influence of the word ஆட்டம் (āṭṭam, “play, game”). Compare also திப்பிலியாட்டம் (tippiliyāṭṭam).
